# Can I compare my samples?

**The question:** before comparing conditions, are the samples themselves
comparable — or is one wildly different? The plot that answers it: the
**distribution of counts per sample**.

First, reshape the counts to *tidy* form (one row per gene × sample) and attach the
sample info:

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
counts_long <- counts %>%
  pivot_longer(-c(gene_id, gene_name), names_to = "sample", values_to = "count") %>%
  left_join(meta, by = "sample")

counts_long
```

A boxplot per sample, coloured by lifestyle (counts are very skewed, so we plot them
on a log scale):

```{r, fig.height=6}
ggplot(counts_long, aes(x = sample, y = log10(count + 1), fill = lifestyle)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "log10(count + 1)")
```

If the boxes line up at similar heights, the samples are comparable. 👍

<div class="remember">
  <strong>📌 Principle:</strong> skewed data (like counts) needs a log scale, or one
  huge value flattens everything else.
</div>

### 👉 Your turn {-}

Show the same information as a **density** plot instead of boxplots: one curve per
sample, coloured by `lifestyle`. (Hint: `geom_density()` with `aes(group = sample)`.)

<details>
<summary>Solution</summary>
```{r, eval=FALSE}
ggplot(counts_long, aes(x = log10(count + 1), group = sample, colour = lifestyle)) +
  geom_density()
```
</details>

> 🤖 **Ask your AI:** *"Why do we add 1 before taking log10 of RNA-seq counts?"*
